options.a: Client with pain 7/10 due for PRN morphine in 30 minutes
options.b: Client with blood glucose 190 mg/dL awaiting lunch
options.c: Client with chronic COPD and SpO2 91% at baseline
options.d: Client with new confusion and SpO2 88% on room air

distractorExplanations.a: Pain needs timely treatment, but it is not a breathing or perfusion threat like new hypoxia with confusion.
distractorExplanations.b: Moderate hyperglycemia before a meal is not immediately life-threatening compared with acute hypoxia.
distractorExplanations.c: An SpO2 of 91% that is this client's COPD baseline is stable; the new drop to 88% with confusion is acute.

options.a: Apply restraints first, then obtain the order within 24 hours
options.b: Obtain verbal consent from family and tie restraints to the side rails
options.c: Obtain a provider order and attempt least-restrictive alternatives
options.d: Obtain a PRN restraint order to use whenever the client is agitated

distractorExplanations.a: Outside true emergencies an order comes first, and even emergency restraint needs an order promptly, not within 24 hours.
distractorExplanations.b: Family consent does not replace a provider order, and restraints are tied to the bed frame, not the side rails.
distractorExplanations.d: PRN (as-needed) restraint orders are not permitted; each episode requires a time-limited order.

options.a: Irrigate the catheter daily with sterile saline to keep the lumen patent
options.b: Replace the catheter every 72 hours on a routine schedule
options.c: Maintain a closed drainage system and keep the bag below the bladder
options.d: Clean the meatus with povidone-iodine every 4 hours

distractorExplanations.a: Routine irrigation breaks the closed system and is not recommended unless ordered for obstruction.
distractorExplanations.b: Catheters are not changed on a fixed schedule; they are removed as soon as no longer needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine meatal care with soap and water is sufficient; frequent antiseptic cleansing does not lower CAUTI.

options.a: Explore the client's concerns and document refusal after education
options.b: Notify the provider and give the dose once an order to proceed is given
options.c: Ask a family member to persuade the client to take it now
options.d: Offer the dose crushed in food so it is easier to swallow

distractorExplanations.b: A provider order cannot override a competent client's refusal; the nurse first explores the reason.
distractorExplanations.c: Using family pressure undermines autonomy; the nurse explores the client's own concerns first.
distractorExplanations.d: Hiding medication in food without consent is covert administration and ignores the refusal.

options.a: A 2-cm bruise on the forearm with full ROM
options.b: New unequal pupils and decreasing LOC
options.c: Mild hip soreness with equal leg length
options.d: Blood pressure 10 mm Hg above baseline

distractorExplanations.a: A small bruise with full range of motion is minor and documented; it does not suggest head injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Soreness with equal leg length and no rotation is less concerning than signs of a possible hip fracture or head injury.
distractorExplanations.d: A small rise in BP after a fall is often from pain or anxiety; neuro changes are the urgent finding.

options.a: Opens the first flap of a package away from the body
options.b: Keeps sterile gloved hands above waist level
options.c: Considers the 1-inch border of the field unsterile
options.d: Turns their back to the sterile field

distractorExplanations.a: Opening the first flap away from the body is correct technique that avoids reaching over the sterile contents.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeping gloved hands above the waist is correct; items below waist level are considered contaminated.
distractorExplanations.c: Treating the outer 1-inch border as unsterile is correct practice, not a break in technique.

options.a: Care for clients on the specialty pumps after watching one setup
options.b: Take the charge nurse role, since it involves fewer pump tasks
options.c: Admit the most acute new client so regular staff can stay with their own
options.d: Care for stable clients with tasks matching general RN competencies

distractorExplanations.a: Watching one setup is not verified competency; float nurses are not assigned unfamiliar specialty equipment.
distractorExplanations.b: Charge duties require knowledge of the unit, its staff, and protocols; they are not given to an unoriented float.
distractorExplanations.c: The most acute, unpredictable clients go to experienced unit staff, not to a float unfamiliar with the specialty.

nclex-rn-readiness-check-safe-care-008.explanation: Float nurses should receive orientation and be assigned within verified competencies. Provide orientation to unit equipment.

options.a: Confirm the client authorized disclosure before sharing PHI
options.b: Share the diagnosis if the visitor is listed as next of kin
options.c: Share general information since the visitor knows the client
options.d: Refer the visitor to the provider, who may share without consent

distractorExplanations.b: Next-of-kin status alone does not authorize disclosure; the client must agree or a legal exception must apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Knowing the client does not create a right to PHI; diagnosis is protected without authorization.
distractorExplanations.d: HIPAA binds providers too; the provider also needs the client's authorization to disclose the diagnosis.

options.a: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN pain
options.b: Normal saline 0.9% IV at 100 mL/hr for maintenance hydration
options.c: Incentive spirometry q1h while awake
options.d: Morphine 50 mg IV push now for a opioid-naive adult

distractorExplanations.b: Normal saline at 100 mL/hr is a common maintenance rate for adults and does not need clarification.
distractorExplanations.a: Standard dosing range.
distractorExplanations.c: Appropriate pulmonary toilet order.

options.a: Activate the fire alarm before moving anyone (RACE)
options.b: Contain the fire by closing doors before moving the client
options.c: Extinguish the fire with the nearest extinguisher first
options.d: Rescue/remove the client from immediate danger (RACE)

distractorExplanations.a: Alarm is the second RACE step; a client in immediate danger is rescued first.
distractorExplanations.b: Containment is the third RACE step, done after rescuing clients and sounding the alarm.
distractorExplanations.c: Extinguishing is the last RACE step and only for small fires after rescue, alarm, and containment.

options.a: Drowsy client 1 hour after receiving IV sedation
options.b: Stable post-op day 2 client asking about activity limits
options.c: Client with uncontrolled pain rated 9/10
options.d: Client newly informed of a cancer diagnosis and crying

distractorExplanations.a: Sedation impairs attention and recall; teaching is delayed until the client is alert.
distractorExplanations.c: Severe uncontrolled pain blocks learning; pain is treated before teaching.
distractorExplanations.d: Acute emotional distress limits readiness to learn; support comes first, with teaching later.

options.a: Objective, factual, and completed per facility policy
options.b: Completed only if the error caused harm to the client
options.c: Objective, with a copy filed in the client's medical record
options.d: Noted in the chart narrative as 'incident report filed'

distractorExplanations.b: No-harm errors and near misses are also reported so systems can be fixed before harm occurs.
distractorExplanations.c: Incident reports are confidential risk-management documents and are not filed in the medical record.
distractorExplanations.d: The chart describes the event and care given but does not reference the incident report itself.

nclex-rn-readiness-check-safe-care-013.explanation: Incident reports are risk-management tools with objective facts; charting focuses on assessment/care without naming the report form. It is usually not referenced in the chart narrative.

options.a: Surgical mask and gloves when entering the room
options.b: Gown and gloves for any contact with the client
options.c: N95 (or higher) respirator when entering the room
options.d: N95 respirator only for aerosol-generating procedures

distractorExplanations.a: A surgical mask is droplet-precaution PPE; TB requires a fit-tested N95 or higher respirator.
distractorExplanations.b: Gown and gloves are contact precautions; airborne precautions require a respirator.
distractorExplanations.d: With suspected TB, the N95 is worn every time staff enter the room, not just during aerosol procedures.

options.a: Verify identity and product with the UAP before spiking the bag
options.b: Prime the tubing with D5W and verify the product at the bedside
options.c: Verify the client's name on the room door sign against the blood bag label
options.d: Verify client identity and blood product with a second qualified person

distractorExplanations.a: UAP are not qualified to perform transfusion verification; a second licensed nurse is required.
distractorExplanations.b: Blood tubing is primed with normal saline; D5W causes hemolysis of red cells.
distractorExplanations.c: A door sign is not an identifier; two identifiers on the client's band are checked against the product.

nclex-rn-readiness-check-safe-care-015.explanation: Two-person verification of client and product is a core transfusion safety step. Follow facility policy.

options.a: Normal fetal movement patterns with sudden marked decrease
options.b: Increased fetal movement after meals compared with the morning
options.c: Fewer than 10 movements per hour during the evening count
options.d: Any day with fewer kicks than the day before, even if slight

distractorExplanations.b: Increased movement after meals is normal and expected; the concern is a marked decrease.
distractorExplanations.c: A common guideline is 10 movements within 2 hours, not 10 per hour, so this threshold is too strict.
distractorExplanations.d: Day-to-day variation is normal; clients report a significant decrease from their baseline pattern.

nclex-rn-readiness-check-health-promo-00.explanation: Clients should know their baby's baseline and report a significant decrease in fetal movement. Each client should know her own pattern.

options.a: Rear-facing car seat and tummy time when awake/supervised
options.b: Forward-facing car seat and tummy time during naps
options.c: Rear-facing car seat and water introduced for hydration
options.d: Rice cereal in the bottle and back-to-sleep positioning

distractorExplanations.b: Infants ride rear-facing, and tummy time is only while awake and supervised, never during sleep.
distractorExplanations.c: Water is not given before about 6 months; breast milk or formula meets hydration needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Cereal in a bottle is a choking and overfeeding risk and is not recommended.

options.a: Rise slowly and report dizziness/syncope
options.b: Stop the drug once BP readings are normal
options.c: Take a double dose if one dose is missed
options.d: Increase salt intake to prevent dizziness

distractorExplanations.b: Normal readings mean the drug is working; stopping causes BP to rise again or rebound.
distractorExplanations.c: Doubling a missed dose risks hypotension; clients follow the missed-dose instructions instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Extra sodium raises blood pressure and counteracts therapy; rising slowly prevents orthostatic dizziness.

options.a: Start annual screening mammograms at age 30 for every average-risk adult
options.b: Skip screening when monthly breast self-exams are normal
options.c: Stop screening after age 50 if one mammogram is normal
options.d: Follow age-based guidelines and discuss personal risk with a provider

distractorExplanations.a: Average-risk screening starts around 40 (USPSTF biennial from 40), not 30; earlier only for high risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Self-exams do not replace mammography; screening detects cancers before they are palpable.
distractorExplanations.c: Screening continues at regular intervals (to about 74 per USPSTF), not stopped after one normal test.

options.a: Can replace prescribed bone medication when done daily
options.b: Should be replaced by swimming to protect fragile bones
options.c: Increases fracture risk and should be limited to stretching
options.d: Can help bone health when cleared by the provider

distractorExplanations.a: Exercise supports bone health but does not replace prescribed osteoporosis drugs.
distractorExplanations.b: Swimming is not weight-bearing and does little for bone density; walking-type activity is preferred.
distractorExplanations.c: Appropriate weight-bearing exercise, cleared by the provider, helps bone and balance; avoiding it accelerates loss.

options.a: Hold the usual insulin dose on any sick day when appetite is poor
options.b: Skip snacks before sports to keep glucose from rising
options.c: Check ketones only when glucose is below 70 mg/dL
options.d: Check glucose and manage carbs/insulin around activity per plan

distractorExplanations.a: Insulin is continued on sick days (often adjusted) because illness raises glucose and DKA risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Exercise lowers glucose, so a carbohydrate snack is often needed before sports to prevent hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.c: Ketones are checked when glucose is high (e.g., above 240 mg/dL) or when ill, not when glucose is low.

options.a: Counseling plus pharmacotherapy when appropriate improves quit rates
options.b: Willpower alone is the most effective evidence-based method for quitting
options.c: E-cigarettes are the first-line FDA-approved cessation aid
options.d: Nicotine patches should not be combined with counseling

distractorExplanations.b: Unaided quitting has the lowest success rates; counseling plus medication works best.
distractorExplanations.c: E-cigarettes are not FDA-approved cessation aids; first-line options are NRT, varenicline, and bupropion.
distractorExplanations.d: Combining NRT with counseling improves quit rates more than either alone.

options.a: Screening is needed only if blood appears in the stool
options.b: Colonoscopy is the sole accepted screening test for average-risk adults
options.c: Screening can stop after one normal stool test at age 50
options.d: Screening options and starting age depend on guidelines and personal risk

distractorExplanations.a: Screening targets people without symptoms; visible blood is a symptom needing diagnostic evaluation.
distractorExplanations.b: Stool-based tests (FIT, stool DNA) and CT colonography are also accepted options.
distractorExplanations.c: Stool tests are repeated at set intervals (FIT yearly), and screening generally continues to age 75.

options.a: Prone on a firm surface to lower the risk of reflux
options.b: Supine on a firm surface, no soft bedding/loose objects
options.c: Side-lying, propped with a rolled blanket for support
options.d: Supine on a firm surface, with crib bumpers for padding

distractorExplanations.a: Prone sleeping increases SIDS risk; healthy infants sleep on their backs.
distractorExplanations.c: Side-lying is unstable and infants can roll prone; rolled blankets are suffocation hazards.
distractorExplanations.d: Crib bumpers are soft objects the AAP advises against due to suffocation and entrapment risk.

options.a: Avoid leafy greens and other vitamin K foods, and keep INR monitoring appointments
options.b: Keep vitamin K intake consistent and keep INR monitoring appointments
options.c: Keep vitamin K consistent and take a double dose if one is missed
options.d: Keep vitamin K consistent and use aspirin for minor aches

distractorExplanations.a: Leafy greens are not avoided; consistent vitamin K intake keeps the INR stable.
distractorExplanations.c: Missed warfarin doses are not doubled; doubling risks bleeding.
distractorExplanations.d: Aspirin adds antiplatelet effect and raises bleeding risk with warfarin; acetaminophen is preferred.

options.a: Hot flashes that disturb sleep
options.b: Vaginal dryness during intercourse
options.c: Irregular periods during perimenopause
options.d: Postmenopausal vaginal bleeding

distractorExplanations.a: Hot flashes are common menopause symptoms managed with lifestyle or therapy, not an urgent warning sign.
distractorExplanations.b: Vaginal dryness is an expected effect of lower estrogen and is treated, not urgently investigated.
distractorExplanations.c: Irregular cycles are expected during perimenopause; bleeding after menopause is what needs evaluation.

options.a: Sun exposure is safe since it does not cause photosensitivity
options.b: Vitamin A supplements boost the drug's effect on acne
options.c: Contraception is needed only during the first month
options.d: Pregnancy prevention requirements are critical

distractorExplanations.a: Isotretinoin increases photosensitivity; clients use sunscreen and limit sun exposure.
distractorExplanations.b: Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative; added vitamin A raises toxicity risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Contraception is required before, during, and for a month after therapy, not just the first month.

nclex-rn-readiness-check-health-promo-01.explanation: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic; pregnancy prevention programs are mandatory. This is due to teratogenicity.

options.a: Encourage fluids only when thirsty, since older adults sense thirst well
options.b: Recommend fans as the main cooling method during extreme heat
options.c: Advise exercise at midday to build heat tolerance quickly
options.d: Encourage hydration and cooling for older adults and outdoor workers

distractorExplanations.a: Older adults have a blunted thirst response, so they should drink regularly before feeling thirsty.
distractorExplanations.b: Fans do not prevent heat illness at very high temperatures; cooled spaces and cooling measures are advised.
distractorExplanations.c: Midday is the hottest period; activity is scheduled for cooler times and acclimatization is gradual.

options.a: Tell me more about what's making you feel like a burden
options.b: Your family loves you, so you are not a burden to them
options.c: Why do you think you feel like a burden to others?
options.d: Let's focus on getting you stronger so you can go home soon

distractorExplanations.b: This is false reassurance that brushes off the feeling instead of exploring it.
distractorExplanations.c: 'Why' questions can feel judgmental and put the client on the defensive; open-ended prompts are preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: This changes the focus to physical goals and avoids the feeling the client expressed.

options.a: Ensure safety (1:1/observation per protocol) and remove means
options.b: Develop a no-suicide contract and check on the client hourly
options.c: Encourage group therapy attendance to reduce isolation
options.d: Ensure privacy in a single room with the door closed

distractorExplanations.b: No-suicide contracts are not evidence-based protection, and hourly checks are too infrequent for an active plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Group therapy is helpful later; immediate safety with close observation comes first.
distractorExplanations.d: Privacy behind a closed door reduces observation; active ideation with a plan needs close or 1:1 observation.

options.a: Document findings and wait for the client to request help
options.b: Report per mandatory reporting laws and ensure immediate safety
options.c: Report only if the client gives consent to the report
options.d: Confront the suspected abuser privately to clarify what happened at home

distractorExplanations.a: Nurses must report suspected elder abuse; waiting for a request leaves the client at risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Mandatory reporting of suspected elder abuse does not depend on the client's consent in most states.
distractorExplanations.d: Confronting the suspected abuser can escalate danger; the nurse reports and ensures safety.

options.a: What messages is the TV sending you about the program?
options.b: Those messages are not real, so there is no reason to be afraid of the TV
options.c: Let's turn off the TV so the messages will stop for now
options.d: I don't hear those messages, but it sounds frightening—you're safe here

distractorExplanations.a: Probing the details of the delusion reinforces it; the nurse focuses on feelings and reality.
distractorExplanations.b: Arguing that the belief is false and dismissing fear does not acknowledge the client's feelings.
distractorExplanations.c: Implying the TV is sending messages supports the delusion instead of presenting reality.

options.a: Expect full mood improvement within the first week of starting therapy
options.b: Take with St. John's wort to speed the antidepressant effect
options.c: Report worsening mood/suicidality, especially early in treatment
options.d: Stop the medication abruptly once mood has improved

distractorExplanations.a: SSRIs usually take 2–6 weeks for full effect; expecting change in a week sets up early discontinuation.
distractorExplanations.b: St. John's wort plus an SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome and is avoided.
distractorExplanations.d: Abrupt stopping can cause discontinuation syndrome and relapse; tapering is done with the provider.

options.a: It's been a year and I can't function, sleep, or leave the house
options.b: I still cry when I see photos of her, six months later
options.c: I still talk to her picture sometimes and it helps me feel close to her
options.d: I sleep poorly some nights, but I'm back at work now

distractorExplanations.b: Crying at reminders months later is part of normal grief and does not indicate impairment.
distractorExplanations.c: Continuing bonds, such as talking to a photo, are a normal coping pattern without functional impairment.
distractorExplanations.d: Occasional poor sleep with return to work shows adaptive functioning, not complicated grief.

options.a: Leave the client alone in a quiet room to regain control
options.b: Coach slow breathing and stay with the client in a calm environment
options.c: Have the client breathe into a paper bag until the tingling and dizziness stop
options.d: Encourage deep, rapid breaths to restore oxygen levels

distractorExplanations.a: An anxious client should not be left alone; staying present helps reduce panic.
distractorExplanations.c: Paper-bag rebreathing is no longer recommended and can cause hypoxia or mask other conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: Rapid breathing worsens hyperventilation and CO2 loss; slow, controlled breaths are coached.

options.a: Mirroring the client's feelings to deepen understanding
options.b: Repeating the client's exact words back to show listening
options.c: Condensing the main points at the end of the talk
options.d: Asking the client to explain an unclear statement

distractorExplanations.b: Repeating the client's words is restating, which echoes content rather than mirroring feelings.
distractorExplanations.c: Condensing key points at the end of a conversation is summarizing, not reflecting.
distractorExplanations.d: Asking for more explanation of an unclear statement is clarifying, a different technique.

options.a: Fine hand tremor and polyuria in the first weeks
options.b: Seizures, coma, and cardiac dysrhythmias
options.c: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, tremor, ataxia
options.d: Metallic taste and mild thirst

distractorExplanations.a: Fine tremor and polyuria are common expected side effects at therapeutic lithium levels.
distractorExplanations.b: Seizures, coma, and dysrhythmias are signs of severe (late) toxicity, not early signs.
distractorExplanations.d: Metallic taste and mild thirst are common side effects, not toxicity.

options.a: Touch the client firmly to bring them back to the present
options.b: Ask the client to describe the traumatic event in detail right away to process it
options.c: Give a PRN sedative before speaking with the client
options.d: Ensure safety, use calm voice, orient to present, reduce stimuli

distractorExplanations.a: Unexpected touch during a flashback can be perceived as a threat and escalate fear or aggression.
distractorExplanations.b: Asking for trauma details during a flashback can retraumatize; grounding in the present comes first.
distractorExplanations.c: Medication is not the first step; calm verbal grounding and a safe environment come first.

options.a: Electrolyte imbalance and cardiac risk from malnutrition
options.b: Body image distortion and intense fear of gaining weight
options.c: Family conflict about the client's eating habits
options.d: Excessive exercise and hiding food at meals

distractorExplanations.b: Body image distortion is a real concern but is addressed after physiologic stability.
distractorExplanations.c: Family dynamics matter in treatment but do not outrank electrolyte and cardiac instability.
distractorExplanations.d: These behaviors are monitored, but physiologic risks such as hypokalemia and dysrhythmias come first.

options.a: Ask what the voices are saying and implement safety precautions
options.b: Tell the client the voices are not real and change the topic
options.c: Seclude the client right away without asking about the voices
options.d: Reassure staff and recheck the client at the end of the shift

distractorExplanations.b: Arguing about reality and changing the subject skips assessing what the commands say.
distractorExplanations.c: Seclusion is a last resort; the nurse first assesses the command content and risk.
distractorExplanations.d: A command to harm staff requires immediate assessment and precautions, not a delayed recheck.

options.a: Expert advice, telling the client the reasons to change
options.b: Confrontation of denial to break through resistance
options.c: Partnership, evoking client's own reasons for change
options.d: Persuasion, arguing for change when the client is unsure

distractorExplanations.a: MI avoids the expert 'righting reflex'; the client's own reasons for change are drawn out.
distractorExplanations.b: Confrontation increases resistance; MI rolls with resistance instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Arguing for change makes ambivalent clients argue against it; MI explores ambivalence.

options.a: Lung sounds, SpO2, and fluid status
options.b: Blood glucose and dietary intake
options.c: Pedal pulses and capillary refill
options.d: Pain level and bowel sounds

distractorExplanations.b: Glucose and diet do not address the acute fluid overload threatening gas exchange.
distractorExplanations.c: Peripheral perfusion checks matter, but dyspnea with weight gain points to lungs and fluid first.
distractorExplanations.d: Pain and bowel sounds are not priority assessments for acute heart failure with dyspnea.

options.a: Peaked T waves and muscle cramps
options.b: Tetany and a positive Chvostek sign
options.c: Dysrhythmias and muscle weakness
options.d: Decreased digoxin toxicity risk

distractorExplanations.a: Peaked T waves are a hyperkalemia ECG change; hypokalemia causes flattened T waves and U waves.
distractorExplanations.b: Tetany and Chvostek sign suggest hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia, not hypokalemia.
distractorExplanations.d: Low potassium increases digoxin toxicity risk rather than reducing it.

options.a: Lower the basal rate and recheck sedation in 1 hour
options.b: Stop PCA, stimulate, support airway/oxygen, notify provider
options.c: Switch to oral opioids since IV doses are too strong
options.d: Let the client rest and recheck respirations and sedation in 4 hours

distractorExplanations.a: RR 8 with poor arousal needs the opioid stopped now; lowering the rate and waiting an hour delays rescue.
distractorExplanations.c: Any opioid worsens respiratory depression; the opioid is stopped and ventilation supported.
distractorExplanations.d: Hard to arouse with RR 8 is respiratory depression, not rest; a 4-hour recheck is dangerous.

nclex-rn-readiness-check-physio-004.explanation: Opioid-induced respiratory depression requires stopping the opioid and supporting ventilation. Follow protocol for airway/oxygen support.

options.a: IV 50% dextrose as the first step
options.b: 15 g fast carbs, recheck glucose ~15 minutes
options.c: Glucagon 1 mg IM, then recheck glucose in 1 hour
options.d: Protein snack, recheck glucose in 1 hour

distractorExplanations.a: IV D50 is for clients who cannot swallow or are unresponsive; conscious clients take oral fast carbs.
distractorExplanations.c: Glucagon is for clients who cannot take oral carbohydrate, and the recheck is at about 15 minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: Protein slows glucose absorption; fast carbs are given first and glucose rechecked in about 15 minutes.

options.a: Turn oxygen up when short of breath, as high as needed
options.b: Use oxygen exactly as prescribed; report worsening dyspnea
options.c: Use oxygen only at night, since daytime use causes dependence
options.d: Remove the cannula during meals and showers to rest the nose

distractorExplanations.a: Self-titrating to high flow can worsen CO2 retention in some COPD clients; use the prescribed rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Oxygen does not cause dependence; it is used for the hours and activities prescribed.
distractorExplanations.d: Meals and showers increase oxygen demand; prescribed oxygen often continues during them.

options.a: Slow the rate and give acetaminophen, then reassess
options.b: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with D5W per protocol
options.c: Stop the transfusion and keep IV open with NS per protocol
options.d: Finish the unit, then notify the blood bank

distractorExplanations.a: Fever, chills, and back pain may signal hemolysis; the transfusion is stopped, not slowed.
distractorExplanations.b: D5W causes hemolysis of red cells; normal saline is the only solution used with blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuing gives more incompatible blood; the transfusion is stopped immediately.

options.a: Low glucose, diaphoresis, and metabolic alkalosis
options.b: Very high glucose with no ketones or acidosis
options.c: High glucose, dehydration, and metabolic acidosis
options.d: High glucose, fluid overload, and respiratory acidosis

distractorExplanations.a: Low glucose with diaphoresis describes hypoglycemia; DKA has high glucose and metabolic acidosis.
distractorExplanations.b: Extreme hyperglycemia without ketosis or acidosis describes HHS, not DKA.
distractorExplanations.d: DKA causes dehydration (not overload) and metabolic, not respiratory, acidosis.

options.a: Air bolus auscultation over the stomach as the sole method of confirmation
options.b: Bubbling when the tube end is placed in a cup of water
options.c: Radiographic confirmation or facility-approved evidence-based method
options.d: Client's ability to speak without coughing after insertion

distractorExplanations.a: Air bolus auscultation is unreliable and cannot distinguish gastric from respiratory placement.
distractorExplanations.b: Placing the tube end in water is an outdated, unreliable test.
distractorExplanations.d: Tubes can enter the airway without coughing or voice change; lack of symptoms does not confirm placement.

options.a: Normal tidaling that shows the lung is re-expanding
options.b: Need to clamp the tube until the bubbling stops
options.c: Possible air leak that needs assessment of system/client
options.d: Expected function of the water-seal chamber

distractorExplanations.a: Tidaling is rise and fall of water with breathing; continuous bubbling indicates an air leak.
distractorExplanations.b: Clamping a chest tube for a leak can cause tension pneumothorax; it is done only briefly to locate leaks per order.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuous bubbling is expected in a wet suction-control chamber, not in the water-seal chamber.

options.a: Thirst and a dry mouth after the dose
options.b: Tinnitus, oliguria, or rash/anaphylaxis signs
options.c: Urine output of 50 mL/hr with clear, pale yellow urine
options.d: Temperature trending down toward normal

distractorExplanations.a: Mild thirst is not a vancomycin toxicity sign; oliguria and tinnitus signal nephro- and ototoxicity.
distractorExplanations.c: Output of 50 mL/hr is adequate (above 30 mL/hr) and shows preserved kidney function.
distractorExplanations.d: A falling fever suggests the infection is responding, which is expected, not a toxicity sign.

options.a: Rate ~60–100, regular, P before each QRS, consistent PR
options.b: Rate 60–100, irregular, with no identifiable P waves
options.c: Rate 40–60, regular, P before each QRS, consistent PR

distractorExplanations.b: An irregular rhythm without identifiable P waves describes atrial fibrillation, not NSR.
distractorExplanations.c: A sinus rhythm at 40–60 is sinus bradycardia; NSR is 60–100.
distractorExplanations.d: A PR interval over 0.20 seconds is first-degree AV block; NSR has a PR of 0.12–0.20 seconds.

options.a: Apply a pressure dressing and recheck in 30 minutes

options.c: Place supine with neck extended to open the airway

distractorExplanations.a: A pressure dressing can worsen airway compression from a hematoma; waiting 30 minutes delays rescue.

distractorExplanations.c: Clients are kept in semi-Fowler's to reduce swelling; neck extension strains the incision.

options.b: Unprescribed NSAIDs that can worsen kidney function
